brief.outcome: Cut software and vendor spend at an 85-person software consultancy from about $46,000 a month to below $36,000 a month within four months, without cancelling anything a client depends on or breaking any team's work.

ambition.goal_beyond: Software spend grows only when a team lead can name what it is for, so costs do not balloon again
rungs: Cancel or downgrade the waste found in today's spend (unused seats, duplicates, abandoned tools)
Find why spend rose from $31,000 to $46,000 (tools bought by individual teams, seat growth, price rises, usage-based charges) and fix how tools are bought and renewed
Keep it true: a renewal calendar built backward from each notice date and a monthly spend check that flags a tool before it renews or a team buys a duplicate
ambition.judge: Ramp transactions and card statements for the real monthly charge (savings count only when the charge stops appearing), Google Workspace sign-in data for who actually uses a tool, and each team lead's written confirmation that the tool is not needed

brief.deliverable: A lower, checked monthly software and vendor bill: confirmed cancellations and downgrades carried out with approval, renegotiated renewals, a renewal calendar, a buying rule for new tools, and a monthly spend readout
done: Spend baseline rebuilt from Ramp and card statements, with annual charges turned into monthly run-rate
A register of tools client delivery depends on, which are never touched
The rise from $31,000 to $46,000 explained by vendor, with every cause marked supported, refuted or unknown
Savings cards ranked; the owner and COO choose
Each cancellation or downgrade has the team lead's written confirmation and the owner's approval before it happens
Run-rate read monthly against the $36,000 target and the guardrails
guardrails: No tool that clients depend on is switched off
Nothing is cancelled without the team lead's written confirmation and the owner's approval
Data is exported before any tool is cancelled
No team reports a blocked client deliverable because a tool was cut
limits: Ramp is read-only; the owner or team leads carry out cancellations and downgrades
Google Workspace admin is used through the browser; no licence is changed without approval
Working data is kept in a Google Sheet
Vendor and employee details stay out of outside searches
brief.technical_level: Not stated; the owner and COO decide, so give ready recommendations to review with plain-language reasons
brief.decides: The owner, together with the COO
unknowns: Renewal dates, notice periods and auto-renew terms for most contracts
Seat counts and real usage per tool
Which tools each team bought and who owns each
What drove the rise from $31,000 to $46,000 (new tools, price rises, seats, usage-based charges)
Whether the $46,000 includes annual or one-off charges, and vendors paid outside Ramp and the cards
Whether any tools are billed on to clients
Whether the AI can read and write the Google Sheet directly

answers.question: Where are you now?
answers.answer: Software and vendor spend about $46,000 a month, up from $31,000 a year ago (card statements and Ramp, reported)

answers.question: Tools and access?
answers.answer: Ramp MCP read-only; Google Workspace admin through the browser

answers.question: How did it happen?
answers.answer: Many tools were bought by individual teams

answers.question: Target and deadline?
answers.answer: Spend below $36,000 a month within four months

answers.question: Rules?
answers.answer: Nothing cancelled without the team lead confirming and the owner's approval; no tool our clients depend on gets switched off

answers.question: Data home and who decides?
answers.answer: Keep data in a Google Sheet; the owner decides with the COO

research.approach: Practitioners start from the raw transactions, not the vendor list: they pull 12 or more months of card and bill-pay data, turn annual and quarterly charges into a monthly run-rate, and bridge last year's figure to this year's by vendor to see what actually rose. They discover tools beyond the card (single sign-on and connected apps, expense reports) and give every tool a named owner. They then test each candidate against real use (last sign-in, active seats), against overlap in function, and against renewal terms, because savings arrive at the notice date, not when someone decides. Client-critical tools are listed first and excluded. Every cancellation or downgrade is confirmed by the owning team lead, data is exported first, and a renewal calendar is built backward from each notice deadline, with a usage review about 90 days ahead. Savings count only when the charge stops appearing in the next statement.

sources.title: Corma: SaaS spend optimization strategies
sources.note: Build a full inventory including SSO apps, card purchases and converted trials; keep a renewal calendar with notice periods and alerts about 90 days before renewal, with an owner for each review and utilization data pulled first; reclaim unused seats and departed users; cut overlapping tools; use usage data to negotiate. Vendor blog.

sources.title: Google Workspace Admin Help: view your users' last sign-in
sources.note: The Admin console Users page shows an approximate last sign-in; 'Hasn't signed in' for new users; data can lag from a couple of hours up to 3 days, so last sign-in is a clue to use, not proof.

sources.title: Zylo: 2026 SaaS Management Index
sources.note: Accessed 2026-11-03; page shows no date. Reports average SaaS spend rising about 8% year over year, AI and usage-priced charges causing unexpected costs (78% of IT leaders), and 61% cutting projects after unplanned SaaS cost increases. Vendor data; the page gives no licence-utilisation figure.

steps.name: Rebuild the spend baseline from raw transactions
steps.why: Annual and one-off charges distort a monthly figure; the baseline must be a run-rate that ties to the statements.

steps.name: Discover every tool and give it an owner
steps.why: Tools bought by individual teams hide outside the card and the vendor list.

steps.name: List the tools clients depend on and exclude them
steps.why: The one thing that must not break is client delivery.

steps.name: Bridge $31,000 to $46,000 by vendor
steps.why: New tools, seat growth, price rises and usage-based charges each need a different fix.

steps.name: Test each tool against real use and overlap
steps.why: Unused seats, departed users and duplicate tools are the safest savings.

steps.name: Build the renewal calendar from notice dates
steps.why: Savings land at the notice deadline; most dates are unknown today.

steps.name: Confirm with team leads, export data, then act with approval
steps.why: Nothing is cancelled without the team lead and the owner, and data is safe first.

steps.name: Read the monthly bill until the charge really stops
steps.why: A decision is not a saving until the statement shows it.

pitfalls.text: Counting a cancellation as a saving before the notice date, or when the charge still appears on the next statement.
Using last sign-in as proof a tool is unused; it is approximate and lags, so a team lead must confirm.
Cutting a tool that a client delivery depends on because it looked quiet.
Missing usage-priced and AI tool charges that vary month to month, so the target is met one month and missed the next.
Treating annual charges as monthly, so the baseline and the target are wrong.

plan.name: Cut software and vendor spend safely

capabilities.why: Pull 13 months of transactions, vendors, cards and cardholders.

capabilities.name: Read users, last sign-in and connected apps (Google Workspace admin)

capabilities.name: Card statements and contract copies (owner)
capabilities.why: Covers vendors paid outside Ramp and gives renewal terms.

capabilities.name: Google Sheet (data home)
capabilities.why: The owner creates and shares the sheet; a CSV copy is kept in this project.

capabilities.name: Send confirmation requests to team leads and negotiation emails to vendors
capabilities.why: Sends messages on the owner's behalf, so each is approved first.

capabilities.why: The owner or team lead carries out each change in the tool or the admin console after both approvals.

data.why: The raw base for the baseline, the bridge from $31,000 and every vendor finding.

Ramp > Transactions > export CSV for the same dates.

data.alternative: With only monthly totals, the bridge by vendor and the run-rate stay unknown.

data.why: Spend by bank transfer or other cards would make the $46,000 incomplete.

Ask the owner whether any vendors are paid by transfer or on other cards.

data.why: Renewal dates are unknown today; savings land at notice dates.

Contract copies and invoices from the owner.

stages.name: Pin down the spend problem
stages.goal: Turn the owner's words into a measured problem, a target, limits and the data we can reach. Writes BRIEF.md.

stages.name: List the tools clients depend on
stages.goal: Ask each team lead which tools support live client work or hold client data, and record them as the do-not-touch register before any savings are looked for.

checks.name: Every team lead has answered, or the team is listed as unanswered and its tools are blocked from cancellation
Each entry names who confirmed it

stages.name: Pull the raw spend and discover the tools
stages.goal: Pull 13 months of transactions, vendors paid outside Ramp, the Workspace user and connected-app lists, and a tool register with owner and contract terms into the Google Sheet and a CSV copy.

checks.name: Monthly totals in the dataset match the Ramp totals and the card statements within 1%
Every tool with a recurring charge has an owner or is listed as unowned
Anything not provided (contracts, off-card vendors, Workspace export) is listed with what it would unlock

stages.name: Rebuild the baseline as a monthly run-rate
stages.goal: Turn annual, quarterly and one-off charges into a monthly run-rate, separate software from other vendors, remove duplicates and refunds, and check the $46,000 and $31,000 figures.

checks.name: Annual and quarterly charges are spread across the months they cover, and one-offs are shown separately
The rebuilt monthly figure is compared with the owner's $46,000 and $31,000, and any difference of more than 5% is explained
Spend is split into software, other vendors and unknown, with unknown under 10% or listed
Ends with CHECKED, LIMITED or UNRELIABLE for the baseline and what that means for the $36,000 target

stages.name: Find why spend rose and what is wasted
stages.goal: Bridge $31,000 to $46,000 by vendor, then test each tool for unused seats, overlap, price rises and usage-based charges, and say how much of any saving lands by month 4 given the renewal dates. Keep competing explanations.

checks.name: The bridge from the year-ago figure to now adds up to the change within 3%, by vendor
Every hypothesis is SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN, with the rows it rests on
Usage claims use at least 60 days of sign-in or seat data and say that last sign-in is approximate
Each saving shows the month it would first show on a statement; savings with unknown renewal dates count as zero toward the 4-month target
No tool on the client-critical register is a candidate

stages.name: Rank the savings
stages.goal: Turn supported findings into ranked savings cards: cancel, downgrade, consolidate or renegotiate, each with monthly saving, first statement month, usage evidence, owning team lead and client risk.

checks.name: Every card cites the finding it rests on
Every card has monthly saving, first statement month, effort, confidence, risk to client work and how it will be measured
The cards that can land within 4 months are summed and compared with the $10,000 a month needed to reach $36,000
No card touches a tool on the client-critical register

stages.name: The owner and COO choose
stages.goal: They pick card IDs. Ask for the reason when they pass over a top card; record it. Choosing a card starts the team-lead check; it does not cancel anything.

checks.name: Chosen and passed-over cards are in decisions.jsonl
A reason is recorded wherever a top card was passed over
The owner's and the COO's decisions are both recorded

stages.name: Prepare the team-lead confirmations and negotiation briefs
stages.goal: For each chosen card, write the confirmation request for the team lead (what, why, usage evidence, what is exported first, deadline) and a negotiation brief for renewals and downgrades.

checks.name: Each request attaches the usage evidence and says plainly that sign-in data is approximate
Each cancellation request lists what data to export first and who does it
Each request states the notice date and the cost of waiting past it

stages.optional_when: No cancellation, downgrade or renegotiation card was chosen.

stages.name: Draft the renewal calendar and the buying rule
stages.goal: Build the renewal calendar backward from each notice date with a named owner and a usage review 90 days ahead, and draft a rule that new tools need a team lead owner and a monthly cost on record.

checks.name: Every tool with a known renewal has a notice date, an owner and a review date 90 days before notice; tools with unknown dates are listed as to-find
The rule fits one page and names who approves a new tool and at what monthly cost

stages.name: Send the confirmation requests and vendor emails
stages.goal: Register the baseline, then send each team-lead confirmation request and each vendor negotiation email only after the owner approves that message. Record replies.

checks.name: Every message has the owner's yes recorded before it is sent
The baseline run-rate and each expected saving are in experiments.jsonl before the first message
Every team-lead reply is recorded as confirmed, declined or no answer; no answer counts as declined

stages.optional_when: No cancellation, downgrade or renegotiation card was chosen.

stages.name: Cancel and downgrade, one tool at a time
stages.goal: For each tool with the team lead's written confirmation, export the data, then show the owner the change and carry it out only after the owner's yes. Read back that the plan and seats changed.

checks.name: Each change has the team lead's written confirmation and the owner's yes on file
Data export is done and checked before cancelling
The tool is not on the client-critical register at the time of the change
The new plan, seat count and next billing date are read back from the vendor or admin console
Each change records how to reverse it and by when

stages.optional_when: No team lead confirmed a change.

stages.name: Read the monthly bill until the charge stops
stages.goal: Each month read the run-rate from Ramp and statements against $46,000, $36,000 and the guardrails, confirm that each saving really left the statement, and flag tools approaching a notice date.

checks.name: A saving is counted only when the charge is absent from the next statement
The monthly figure uses the same run-rate method as the baseline
Reported blocked deliverables and restored tools are counted
The target counts as met only after two consecutive months with run-rate below $36,000

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Close each experiment, save rules with their scope, and plan the next round.

checks.name: Every registered experiment is closed in experiments.jsonl with a verdict
Each rule says whether it holds for one tool, this company or the playbook

hypotheses.statement: Tools bought by individual teams in the last year explain most of the rise.
hypotheses.test: Vendors whose first charge is within the last 12 months, by team; their share of the $15,000 increase.
hypotheses.confirm_if: New vendors account for 50% or more of the increase.
hypotheses.refute_if: New vendors account for under 20% of the increase.

hypotheses.statement: Several teams pay for tools that do the same job.
hypotheses.test: Group tools by function (project tracking, design, docs, AI assistants, monitoring); count paid tools per function.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Three or more functions have two or more paid tools, with consolidation worth at least $2,000 a month.

hypotheses.statement: A meaningful share of paid seats are unused.
hypotheses.test: Paid seats against active users (last sign-in within 60 days, vendor admin data, team lead check).
hypotheses.confirm_if: 15% or more of paid seats on the top 20 tools are inactive for 60 days.

hypotheses.statement: Price rises at renewal, not new tools, drive part of the increase.
hypotheses.test: Monthly charge per vendor over time compared with seat count.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Charges for the same vendors rose 10% or more with no seat growth, and explain 25% or more of the increase.

hypotheses.statement: Usage-based and AI tool charges vary month to month and inflate the bill.
hypotheses.test: Month-to-month swing and growth in usage-priced vendors (AI assistants, cloud tools, APIs).
hypotheses.confirm_if: Usage-priced vendors rose 20% or more in the last 6 months or swing more than 20% a month, and make up 20% or more of the increase.
hypotheses.refute_if: They are stable and under 10% of the increase.

hypotheses.statement: The $46,000 is distorted by annual or one-off charges.
hypotheses.test: Spread annual and quarterly charges over the months they cover.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The rebuilt run-rate differs from $46,000 by more than 5%.

hypotheses.statement: Tools linger after the project or the person is gone.
hypotheses.test: Subscriptions whose cardholder left or whose users have not signed in for 90 days.
hypotheses.confirm_if: At least 5 subscriptions or $1,000 a month fit this.

hypotheses.statement: Many contracts renew too late in the year for savings to land within 4 months.
hypotheses.test: Renewal and notice dates against the 4-month window.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Savings that can land within 4 months total less than $10,000 a month.
hypotheses.refute_if: They total $10,000 a month or more.

hypotheses.statement: Some cheap-looking candidates support client work.
hypotheses.test: Cross-check candidates with the client-critical register and team lead answers.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Any candidate appears on the register or a team lead objects.

measurement.window: Four months, read monthly from Ramp and card statements with the same run-rate method; savings counted when the charge is absent from the next statement.
measurement.min_volume: Two consecutive months with run-rate below $36,000 before the target is called met; one month is a data point.
measurement.stop_rule: Restore a tool within one business day if a team reports a blocked client deliverable, and stop further cancellations after two such cases until the owner reviews.
